messages.author: 921babf3116f4be1
messages.subject: Determine Estimator in Lavaan
parts:
Hi together,

I am doing a CFA with 7-point Likert Scale Data and therefore want to change the estimator from ML to diagonally weighted least squares (DWLS). I am not very familiar with R and I am using the Lavaan Package in SPSS. I could not figure out in which place I have to insert the estimator = "DWLS" section. Could you help me?

My code looks like this:
SPSS2LAVAAN modelspec =
'RelativerVorteil=~ REV1 + REV2 + REV3 + REV4 + REV5 + REV6 + REV7 + REV8'
'Image =~ IMG1 + IMG2 + IMG3'
'Kosten =~ KOS1 + KOS2 + KOS3 + KOS4'
'Kompatbilität =~ KOM1 + KOM2 + KOM3'
'Benutzerfreundlichkeit  =~ BEN1 + BEN2 + BEN3 + BEN4 + BEN5 + BEN6'
'Netzwerkeffekte  =~ NEZ1+ NEZ2 + NEZ3 + NEZ4 + NEZ5'
'Sicherheit =~ SIC1 + SIC 2 + SIC3 + SIC4 + SIC5'
'Transaktionsgeschwindigkeit =~ TRA1 + TRA2 + TRA3'
/output FIT.MEASURES = TRUE.

Best Regards
Marin

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Determine Estimator in Lavaan
parts: I am doing a CFA with 7-point Likert Scale Data and therefore want to change the estimator from ML to diagonally weighted least squares (DWLS).

Why?  It is pretty much universally accepted that 7-point Likert data approximate a continuum closely enough to provide unbiased results when using robust ML estimation (estimator = "MLR" or "MLM"):

http://psychmodels.ucdavis.edu/uploads/8/6/3/9/86398102/rhemtullabrosseauliardsavalei_pm.pdf

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-015-0619-7
I could not figure out in which place I have to insert the estimator = "DWLS" section. Could you help me?

I've never seen this before, but look for the ESTIMATOR argument in the documentation:

https://www.statistik-verstaendlich.de/spss2lavaan/hilfe-fuer-spss2lavaan-version-0-1/

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Hi Terrence

Many thanks for your reply. The documentation link helped me to check the DWLS estimator for my survey data.

Regarding the "right" estimator for 7-point likert scale data: The problem is that several fit indices do not indicate good model fit (cfi, tli, rmsea, srmr) with my data in my bachelor thesis if I use MLR or MLM. So I started researching if other estimators would
make sense too for my model (and get me a better model fit).

I have read your referenced journal articles as well, thank you for providing them.

"When Can Categorical Variables Be Treated as Continuous? A Comparison of Robust Continuous and Categorical SEM Estimation Methods Under Suboptimal Conditions"
  • recommend cat-LS for data sets containing variables with fewer than 5 categories and ML when there are 5 or more categories, sample size is small, and category thresholds are approximately symmetric.
  • With 6 –7 categories, results were similar across methods for many conditions; in these cases, either method is acceptable.
"Confirmatory factor analysis with ordinal data: Comparing robust maximum likelihood and diagonally weighted least squares"
  • each estimator has its advantages and disadvantages
  • study provides conclusive evidence that WLSMV performs uniformly better than MLR in factor loading estimates across all experimental conditions
My conculsion: Based on your sources,  I could also use DWLS for my 7-point liker scale (sample size: 230 participants) to get a better model fit instead of ML. Is that correct?

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Determine Estimator in Lavaan
parts: My conculsion: Based on your sources,  I could also use DWLS for my 7-point liker scale (sample size: 230 participants) to get a better model fit instead of ML. Is that correct?

No, you do not choose an estimator based on its resulting fit indices.  ML and DWLS don't even use the same criteria (covariance matrix and mean vector vs. polychoric correlation matrix and thresholds), so the fit is not comparable across estimators.

N=230 is far too small for even a small model for DWLS to provide stable results, especially with so many categories.  If your model is large, 230 might still be small for ML, but it shouldn't be as bad as DWLS.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
